title: Ed Tech's 5% Problem
author: Rick Hess
summary: Rick Hess interviews Michael Horn about why AI tutors keep posting disappointing school results even as the models themselves improve. The framing device is Laurence Holt's 5% problem: the tools may work well for the small share of students who use them as recommended, and almost nobody else opens them. Horn's answer is that this is a motivation and accountability problem rather than a product problem, and he invokes Daniel Willingham on minds wired to take the path of least resistance and Nat Malkus on districts that still cannot get students to show up. The move the piece makes is to put the learning model ahead of the technology: dropped into a conventional classroom, a tutor can only be an add-on, and it often collides with existing routines and goes unused. Horn's remedy is structural, such as a station-rotation block that guarantees every student hits minimum usage, plus accountability for mastery rather than logged time. He credits Alpha School for at least having a coherent theory of motivation while doubting its premise that academic work cannot itself be rewarding.
points: Holt's 5% figure reframes uneven AI tutoring results as a usage problem rather than evidence that the tutors do not work.
Horn argues technology crammed into an unchanged classroom model can make teaching more efficient but cannot reinvent it, and often conflicts with existing routines.
A station-rotation block is offered as the cheapest fix because scheduled, uninterrupted time makes minimum usage automatic.
Accountability should attach to mastering material rather than to time logged on a device.
Alpha School earns qualified credit for baking a theory of motivation into its model rather than bolting one on afterward.
quotes: The big, recurring problem is that only a small share of students use them as recommended . Laurence Holt has dubbed this the 5% problem .
Michael: Rick, put yourself in the shoes of a teenager. Do you want to do hard work if there's no clear connection between the effort and an outcome you actually care about?

As your AEI colleague Nat Malkus has shown , many schools are still struggling just to get students to show up consistently-and we somehow expect those same students to voluntarily fire up an AI-powered tutor with no human accountability attached to it?
Our minds are wired to take the path of least resistance. Given the chance to avoid hard work, most of us take it.
First off, we too often start with the technology and discount the learning model itself. Technology isn't a silver bullet in education.
Here's one conclusion: Before focusing on the technology, we need to redesign the learning model itself.
We can require students to use technology, but we can't require that they use it well.

First, students have to be accountable for actually mastering the material, not just logging time. Second, a model needs a coherent theory of motivation baked into it, rather than bolted on as an afterthought.
